title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook & Benchmarking Suite
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical serving runtime reference for Redwood Inference covering: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling heuristics, the profiling and benchmarking playbooks, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and pointers for the team wiki. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams and for partner onboarding docs used by solutions engineers.

Sections covered:
- Runtime architecture and core components
- Kernel scheduling model and configurable policies
- Profiling playbook (how to collect, analyze, and act)
- Benchmarking suite (workloads, metrics, and reproducible commands)
- Release notes (latest stable release summary)
- Known issues and workarounds
- Runtime runbooks and incident procedures
- Team wiki links and ownership

1) Runtime architecture 

Short intro: the serving runtime (service name: runtime-service) is a GPU-optimized inference engine that provides request routing, batching, KV cache management, kernel selection, and model variant fallbacks. It is composed of the following core components:

- runtime-api: REST/GRPC front-end used by the Redwood API gateway.
- scheduler-service: policy engine that implements latency/cost/region routing and batch assembly.
- kernel-scheduler: per-GPU process that chooses kernels, CUDA streams and dispatch order based on model graph and request mix.
- kv-cache: low-latency prefix + KV caching layer backed by Redis (local LRU + shared cluster) for prompt caching.
- telemetry-agent: collects traces, histograms, and counters (exports to Prometheus/Tempo/Influx).
- model-loader: handles pinned versioning, warm-start, and eviction.

Key architecture notes:
- Model execution is orchestrated across GPU worker processes with shared memory for KV caches to reduce copy overhead.
- Kernel selection uses a two-stage decision: static profile lookup (compiled kernel table) followed by dynamic heuristics that adjust for sequence length, batch size and observed latency.
- Continuous batching runs on the scheduler-service; kernel-scheduler receives assembled micro-batches and is responsible for stream assignment to avoid head-of-line blocking.

SLOs and targets:
- Global P95 latency target for text generation (seq len 256): <= 120ms (99th percentile <= 350ms for hosted tier).
- Throughput target (Dedicated medium pool, 8x A100): ~12k tokens/s aggregate for default model set.
- Cache hit target: >= 35% for high-traffic prefix-heavy workloads.
- Availability: 99.9% uptime for Dedicated pools (measured per calendar month).

Ownership: runtime-service (primary), eng-serving-runtime (team), oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com.

2) Kernel scheduling model

Concepts:
- Continuous batching: accumulate requests up to max_batch_size or max_latency_ms before dispatch.
- Sub-batching: for very large models we split batches across multiple streams to keep GPU SM utilization high.
- Kernel selection table: compiled per-model architecture with preferred kernels for specific sequence lengths and quantization profiles.
- Preemption/eviction: best-effort preemption is implemented for latency-sensitive tiers using CUDA stream priorities and inflight cancellation tokens.

Configurable policy knobs (short list):
- scheduling.mode: latency_first | throughput_first | balanced
- max_batch_size: integer (default 64)
- max_latency_ms: integer (default 20)
- stream_concurrency: integer (default 2)
- kernel_selector_timeout_ms: integer (default 5)

Scheduler heuristics details:
- latency_first: prioritize small batches, aggressive sub-batching, and faster but lower-flops kernels.
- throughput_first: increase batching window, prefer high-throughput fused kernels and FP16/quantized paths.
- balanced: dynamic switching based on moving-window latency and token-per-second targets.

Table: kernel scheduling config (example)
| param | default | description |
| scheduling.mode | balanced | High-level tradeoff between latency and throughput |
| max_batch_size | 64 | Max requests grouped into a single kernel dispatch |
| max_latency_ms | 20 | Max time scheduler waits before forcing a dispatch |
| stream_concurrency | 2 | Number of CUDA streams used per model worker |
| kernel_selector_timeout_ms | 5 | Time budget to pick a kernel variant before falling back |

3) Profiling playbook (how to collect, triage, and fix)

Purpose: provide a reproducible process for performance regressions and latency spikes. Follow this playbook for any production or staging performance anomaly.

Preflight (collect context):
1. Record incident window and affected endpoints (route/model).
2. Note SLOs breached and percent of traffic impacted.
3. Capture git SHA of runtime-service and model version.

Data collection steps:
1. Increase telemetry sampling to 100% for the affected pool for 10 minutes (use telemetry-agent --set-sampling 100 --pool <pool-id>).
2. Collect CPU/GPU traces: run nv-nsight or perf-collector on an affected worker (example):
   - sudo perf-collector collect --target runtime-worker-23 --duration 120 --output /tmp/trace.tgz
   - nsight-sys --capture-range=pid:$(pidof runtime-worker) --output=/tmp/nsight-report.qs
3. Export kernel-level breakdown from kernel-scheduler:
   - curl -s http://scheduler-service:9090/api/v1/kernels?worker=runtime-worker-23 > /tmp/kernels.json
4. Pull Prometheus histograms for latency, batch sizes, stream stalls and gpu_util:
   - curl -s "http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query_range?query=runtime_latency_bucket{pool=\"<pool-id>\"}&start=...&end=..." > /tmp/latency.json

Analysis checklist:
- Check batch size distribution for an increase in very small batches (indicator of head-of-line or misrouted traffic).
- Inspect kernel selection changes: did runtime fall back to a slower kernel variant (quantization mismatch or kernel selection timeout)?
- Compare GPU SM utilization vs. launch latency; low utilization with high launch overhead suggests kernel launch / serialization issues.
- Review KV-cache hit rates; sudden drop often explains increased token work.

Common fixes and mitigations:
- If small batches: lower scheduling.max_latency_ms temporarily to force batching behavior or change routing to isolate small-latency requests.
- If kernel fallback: increase kernel_selector_timeout_ms or restore last-known-good kernel table and roll model variant back.
- If GPU saturation: scale pool (add worker) or switch to throughput_first and increase max_batch_size.

4) Benchmarking suite 

Purpose: provide reproducible benchmarks for PRs and releases. Suite name: runtime-bench v3. Contains unit workloads and production-mimicking traces.

Environments supported: A100-40GB, H100-80GB, and a 4xA10x GPU multi-slot config for Dedicated pricing sims.

Included workloads:
- micro-latency: single request P95/P99 for seq len 64/256/1024.
- throughput: sustained token/sec for 60s with synthetic parallel clients.
- cache-hit sim: prefix-heavy traffic to measure KV cache benefits.
- mixed-tenant: 50/30/20 split of latency-sensitive/throughput/background tenants.

How to run (example commands):
- setup: source infra/envs/runtime-bench-a100.env
- run latency test: ./bench/run_latency.py --model redwood-llama-13b --seq 256 --concurrency 16 --duration 30 --out /tmp/latency.json
- run throughput test: ./bench/run_throughput.py --model redwood-llama-13b --batch-size 64 --gpu-workers 8 --duration 60

Pass/fail criteria for PR gating:
- No regression > 5% in P95 over branch baseline for latency-critical models.
- Token/sec regression <= 8% for throughput tests (unless flagged and reviewed).

Artifacts and CI integration:
- Bench results uploaded to bench-db (S3: s3://redwood-bench/runtime/v3/<build-id>/).
- PR must include bench diff links. Large regressions require a perf owner sign-off.

5) Release notes (stable release 2029-03-01, v2.8.0)

Summary: v2.8.0 focuses on kernel-selector improvements and a new dynamic batching policy. Key changes:
- kernel-scheduler: improved heuristic for short-sequence kernels, reduced kernel selection latency by ~18%.
- scheduler-service: added scheduling.mode=balanced which dynamically shifts between latency_first and throughput_first.
- telemetry-agent: added kernel-level histograms and per-kernel tail latency metrics.
- bugfix: resolved memory leak in model-loader when unloading quantized checkpoints.

Upgrade notes:
1. Rolling upgrade supported: deploy runtime-service v2.8.0 with scheduler-service v2.8.0.
2. If using custom kernel tables, run: ./tools/compile_kernels --input custom-table.yaml --validate before upgrade.
3. Monitor P95/P99 closely for first 30 minutes and be ready to rollback on >10% sustained regression.

6) Known issues (truncated list)

- ISSUE-2029-014: rare kernel selector timeout on H100 with sequence lengths > 4096. Impact: occasional fallback to slower kernel variant, increased tail latency. Workaround: set kernel_selector_timeout_ms=15 for affected pools.
- ISSUE-2029-021: KV-cache stale hits after model reload causing transient latency spikes. Workaround: force kv-cache flush during model rollout: curl -X POST http://kv-cache:8080/flush?model=<model-id>.
- ISSUE-2028-199: telemetry-agent high CPU at 100% when sampling at 100% on older worker types. Workaround: limit sampling window to 5-10 minutes and capture targeted perf traces.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident response)

Runbook: High P95 latency on hosted API
1. Triage: check /status page and runtime telemetry dashboards (SLO, P95, P99, batch-size distribution).
2. Identify impacted pool and model from route -> pool mapping (service: scheduler-service route table).
3. Short mitigation (5–15m): change scheduling.mode to latency_first for the affected pool:
   - curl -X POST http://scheduler-service:9090/api/v1/pool/<pool-id>/config -d '{"scheduling.mode":"latency_first"}'
4. If kernel fallback suspected: revert to previous kernel table:
   - ./tools/deploy_kernel_table --pool <pool-id> --table /opt/kernel-tables/previous.json
5. If GPU saturation: scale up pool by adding 2 workers via autoscaler UI or CLI.
6. If incident persists >30m: open incident and escalate to oncall lead, prepare rollback to runtime-service v2.7.x.
7. Post-incident: run profiling playbook and create a postmortem with root cause, mitigation, and owner.

Runbook: Worker OOMs after model load
1. Evict recent model loads: use model-loader API to unload non-critical model versions.
2. Temporarily reduce prewarm replicas to 0 for the pool.
3. Increase worker memory or use larger GPU instances for large quantized checkpoints.

Appendix: Useful commands
- Dump scheduler state: curl http://scheduler-service:9090/api/v1/state | jq . > /tmp/scheduler-state.json
- Force cache flush: curl -X POST http://kv-cache:8080/flush?model=<model-id>
- Collect nsight: nsight-sys --capture-range=cpu:pid:$(pidof runtime-worker) --output /tmp/nsight.qs --sampling=1ms --duration=120
